(CNN)  -- Two former presidents reflected on their greatest regrets in office Monday, each looking back to issues that continue to plague the nation years later. Former presidents and political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush now share philanthropic efforts. Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana. Asked his biggest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to get Saddam Hussein to leave office at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991. He told the gathering, "I've thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn't do that." But he said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after he was captured has made him reconsider. Bush recalled their talk, "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have." Bush said, "We ended it the way we said we would" as a military success, but noted a cleaner ending "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have been avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him." On a day that President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed the failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians. "My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted. "If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over West Bank then than they do today," Clinton said. "And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors." Clinton said a deal would have helped the U.S. handle other issues in the region, saying, "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that. " Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to "stop the Rwandan genocide," and succeeding on a new health care plan. He said "presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made" with historians, because it teaches lessons. He said he shared problems during the lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, saying, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones." Clinton added, "all of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them aren't right."

**NEW ORLEANS (CNN)** — In a joint appearance before the National Automobile Dealers Association, former presidents—and former political rivals—George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton reflected on their greatest regrets in office. Now united by shared philanthropic endeavors, the two statesmen looked back on pivotal decisions surrounding geopolitical issues that continue to resonate today.

When asked about his primary regret upon leaving office, President Bush revealed that he often ponders whether he should have pressed for Saddam Hussein’s surrender or removal at the conclusion of the 1991 Gulf War. 

"I've thought a lot about it," Bush remarked, explaining that at the end of Operation Desert Storm, the central dilemma was whether Allied forces should have "kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn't do that."

However, a subsequent conversation with the FBI agent who interrogated the captured Iraqi dictator prompted Bush to reconsider. Recalling their discussion, Bush noted: "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have."

While affirming that "we ended it the way we said we would" as a decisive military success, Bush acknowledged that a cleaner resolution "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him."

Speaking on a day when President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as his special envoy, President Clinton reflected on his own failure to achieve lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians. 

"My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted," Clinton stated. 

He underscored the magnitude of the missed opportunity, noting that his administration had overseen seven years of incremental progress toward peace. This included 1998—the only year in Israel's history without a single casualty from a terrorist attack—as well as a period when Palestinians exercised greater control over the West Bank than they do today.

"If he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors," Clinton said. He maintained that such an agreement would have significantly strengthened the U.S. position in addressing other regional issues: "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that."

In addition to the Middle East, Clinton cited his failure to do more to "stop the Rwandan genocide" and his inability to pass a national healthcare reform plan as major regrets. 

Reflecting on the broader nature of leadership, Clinton emphasized that former chief executives should candidly share their missteps with historians so that future leaders might learn from them. Recalling a recent luncheon between President Obama and the four living former presidents where these challenges were discussed, Clinton noted, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones."

He concluded with a pragmatic observation on executive decision-making: "All of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them that aren't right."

### Echoes of Decision: Bush and Clinton Reflect on the Regrets That Shaped the Modern World

In a rare and candid joint question-and-answer forum, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton stepped away from political rhetoric to offer a profound reflection on the burdens of executive leadership. Sharing a stage as elder statesmen whose once-fierce political rivalry had transformed into a deep personal friendship, the two leaders addressed a range of pressing national and foreign policy issues. However, the most striking moment of the evening came when both men turned their focus backward, acknowledging the critical foreign policy regrets that continue to cast long shadows over global politics today.

For George H.W. Bush, the 41st president, his greatest regret stemmed from the outcome of the 1991 Gulf War. Operation Desert Storm had been a resounding military victory, successfully swift in driving Saddam Hussein’s Iraqi forces out of occupied Kuwait and assembling an unprecedented global coalition. Yet, Bush lamented his administration's decision to halt the military advance once Kuwait was liberated, rather than pressing forward into Baghdad to force Hussein’s total surrender or removal from power. At the time, Bush had strictly adhered to the United Nations mandate and feared the lingering quagmire of an American occupation. Looking back, however, he acknowledged that leaving Hussein in power allowed the dictator to brutally suppress internal uprisings, destabilize the region for another decade, and ultimately set the stage for the second U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003—a conflict championed by his own son, George W. Bush, which drastically altered the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East.

Bill Clinton, reflecting on his two terms in the White House during the 1990s, pointed to a very different kind of missed opportunity: the failure to secure a lasting peace in the Middle East. Clinton spoke with visible emotion about the intense, late-night diplomacy of the 2000 Camp David Summit, where he sought to bridge the gap between Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat. Clinton considered his inability to persuade Arafat to accept a historic proposal for a two-state solution to be the single greatest frustration of his presidency. The offer, which included a Palestinian state in the vast majority of the West Bank and Gaza Strip with a capital in East Jerusalem, was rejected by Arafat without a counterproposal. Clinton reflected on how the breakdown of those negotiations sparked the violent Second Intifada, destroyed the Israeli-Palestinian peace consensus, and ushered in decades of renewed violence that continues to consume the region today.

By sharing these deeply personal admissions, Bush and Clinton illustrated a sobering truth about the presidency: the choices made—or left unmade—in the Oval Office often carry consequences that extend far beyond a single commander-in-chief's tenure. 

Their dialogue provided the audience with more than just a history lesson; it offered a masterclass in the unintended consequences of global statesmanship. As current foreign policy challenges loom large on the world stage, the candid reflections of these two former leaders serve as a poignant reminder that modern history is shaped not only by a nation's military and diplomatic triumphs, but also by the haunting "what ifs" of missed opportunities.

**CNN.com**

**Former rivals, unlikely friends: Bush and Clinton reflect on their biggest presidential regrets in New Orleans**

**By CNN Political Staff**
**Updated 8:42 PM ET, Thu October 18, 2007**

**NEW ORLEANS (CNN) —** On the same stage where they once battled for the nation’s highest office, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton offered a striking display of post-presidential unity Thursday evening in New Orleans, engaging in a deeply personal discussion about the burdens of the Oval Office—and the decisions that still haunt them.

Speaking to a packed audience of students, civic leaders, and hurricane survivors at a joint leadership forum in the Crescent City, the 41st and 42nd presidents put aside the partisan bitterness that defined the 1992 election. Instead, they shared a candid exchange about the triumphs, missteps, and heavy costs of the presidency.

When asked by the moderator to name their single biggest regret from their time in the White House, both men bypassed easy talking points to offer somber, introspective answers.

### Bush: The political cost of compromise

For George H.W. Bush, the reflection turned to the infamous 1988 campaign pledge that came back to haunt his presidency: "Read my lips: no new taxes."

"I made a promise to the American people, and politically, breaking it was the biggest mistake of my career," Bush told the quieted room. "In 1990, the country was facing a massive deficit. I had to sit down with a Democratic Congress, and we had to compromise. I had to raise revenues to save the economy."

Bush, 83, admitted that while he believed the budget deal was the right move for the long-term stability of the nation, the rhetoric he used during the campaign left a mark he never quite recovered from politically.

"I hated breaking my word," Bush said, looking toward Clinton with a wry smile. "And a guy sitting right next to me made sure I paid for it in 1992. But seriously, standing by that pledge cost me a second term. If I had it to do over again, I would have phrased it differently—or not given a soundbite that boxed me into a corner."

### Clinton: The shadow of inaction

When the question turned to Clinton, the 42nd president bypassed domestic political squabbles and pointed to what he called the darkest failure of his foreign policy: the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

"Without a doubt, my biggest regret was not acting faster, or more forcefully, when the killings began in Rwanda," Clinton said, his voice dropping an octave. "We were still reeling from what had happened to our troops in Somalia just months prior, and the intelligence was fragmented. But that’s no excuse."

Over the course of roughly 100 days in 1994, an estimated 800,000 Hutus and Tutsis were slaughtered. Clinton recalled visiting Kigali years later to personally apologize to the survivors.

"If we had sent even a modest force, we could have saved tens of thousands, maybe hundreds of thousands of lives," Clinton said. "I think about it all the time. As president, you realize that your decisions—and your indecision—carry a body count. That failure is something I will carry with me for the rest of my life."

### A bond forged in the Big Easy

The sight of the two former commanders-in-chief sharing a stage in New Orleans held deep symbolism. Once bitter political enemies, the pair forged an unexpected and close friendship in the wake of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and, more recently, Hurricane Katrina. 

Together, they raised tens of millions of dollars for the Gulf Coast through the Bush-Clinton Katrina Fund, frequently visiting the region to inspect rebuilding efforts. Their tight bond has famously prompted Bush’s wife, former First Lady Barbara Bush, to joke that Clinton has become like a "brother from another mother" to her children.

Throughout the two-hour event, the warmth between the two men was palpable. Clinton praised Bush’s foreign policy during the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Gulf War, calling him "one of the most underappreciated foreign policy presidents in American history." Bush, in turn, praised Clinton’s economic stewardship in the 1990s and his relentless energy in post-presidential humanitarian work.

### Advice for a polarized nation

As the event drew to a close, the discussion shifted to the current political climate in Washington. Both former presidents expressed concern over deepening partisan divides as the 2008 presidential race heats up.

"When Bill and I ran against each other, it was tough. We went at it," Bush said. "But at the end of the day, we respected the institution, and we respected each other. Today, the debate feels far more toxic."

Clinton echoed the sentiment, urging the audience—and the next generation of leaders—to seek common ground, even when discussing the hardest topics.

"You can’t govern a country as big and diverse as America from the fringes," Clinton said. "You have to be willing to sit down with people you disagree with, listen to them, and accept that you might be wrong about a few things. George and I proved that you can fight like hell for what you believe in, and still end up best friends."

**ECHOES OF HISTORY: BUSH AND CLINTON REFLECT ON FOREIGN POLICY REGRETS IN RARE JOINT APPEARANCE**

**PHILADELPHIA** — In a rare and candid joint appearance, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton shared a stage on Thursday evening to reflect on the immense burdens of the Oval Office, offering a deeply personal look at the foreign policy decisions that continue to haunt their respective legacies.

Speaking before a packed auditorium of diplomats, historians, and students, the 41st and 42nd presidents—once fierce political rivals turned close personal friends—abandoned traditional talking points to engage in a nuanced discussion on the limits of American power. From the sands of the Middle East to the hills of Rwanda, both men acknowledged the painful gap between diplomatic ambition and geopolitical reality.

### Bush on Saddam Hussein: The Weight of an Unfinished Reckoning

For George H.W. Bush, whose presidency was defined by the sweeping military success of the 1991 Persian Gulf War, the conversation inevitably turned to Iraq and its ousted dictator, Saddam Hussein.

While Bush firmly defended his decision to end Operation Desert Storm once Kuwait was liberated—adhering strictly to the United Nations mandate—he expressed profound, lingering remorse over the immediate aftermath. By choosing not to march on Baghdad and depose Saddam, the U.S. left the dictator in power, allowing him to brutally suppress subsequent uprisings by Iraqi Shia and Kurdish populations.

"We accomplished our mission, and we built a truly global coalition to stand up to aggression," Bush told the audience, his voice measured. "But you cannot look back at the suffering of the Kurds, or the Marsh Arabs who believed we would back them to the end, without feeling a heavy weight. Leaving Saddam in place to terrorize his own people for another decade... that is something that stays with you. You ask yourself if you made the right call for the long term."

Bush noted that while an full-scale invasion in 1991 would have fractured the international coalition and mired American troops in an urban quagmire—a prophecy that would later confront his son, President George W. Bush—the human cost of leaving Saddam in power remained one of his most agonizing strategic trade-offs.

### Clinton on Rwanda: "Our Utter Failure to Act"

When the moderator turned to Bill Clinton, the 42nd president did not hesitate when asked about his single greatest foreign policy regret. 

"Rwanda," Clinton said quietly, referring to the 1994 genocide in which an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus were slaughtered in just 100 days. "It was the ultimate systemic and moral failure of my administration."

Clinton reflected on how the recent loss of U.S. soldiers in Mogadishu, Somalia—the infamous "Black Hawk Down" incident in late 1993—had left Washington and the international community risk-averse and paralyzed. That hesitation, Clinton admitted, blinded his administration to the sheer scale of the horror unfolding in Central Africa.

"We were so focused on the shadow of Somalia that we failed to see the catastrophe right in front of us," Clinton said, leaning forward. "If we had introduced even a modest force—a few thousand troops—we could have saved hundreds of thousands of lives. I think about it all the time. It was a failure of imagination, a failure of leadership, and my deepest regret in public life."

### The Middle East: Clinton’s Frustration with Arafat

The discussion then shifted to the Middle East peace process, where Clinton offered a searing assessment of the collapsed 2000 Camp David Summit. Clinton had spent the final months of his presidency attempting to broker a historic peace deal between Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian Liberation Organization (PLO) Chairman Yasser Arafat.

Barak had made unprecedented concessions, offering a two-state solution that included a Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, with a capital in East Jerusalem. However, Arafat ultimately rejected the proposal without offering a counter-proposal, leading to the eruption of the Second Intifada shortly after.

"I believed then, and I believe today, that peace was within our grasp," Clinton said, detailing the grueling, sleep-deprived negotiations. "Ehud Barak took enormous political risks. But Arafat simply could not make the leap from being a revolutionary leader to being a statesman responsible for building a nation."

Clinton recalled his final, tense phone call with the Palestinian leader. "Arafat called me a great man," Clinton recounted to the audience. "And I told him, 'I am not a great man. I am a failure, and you made me one.' He missed a historic opportunity that would have given the Palestinian people the state they deserved, and the region has paid the price ever since."

### A Bond Forged in the Shadow of the Presidency

Despite the somber nature of the topics, the warmth between the two former commanders-in-chief was palpable throughout the evening. Their post-presidential partnership—which began when President George W. Bush enlisted them to lead humanitarian relief efforts following the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and Hurricane Katrina—has become a model of cross-party civility.

Closing the session, Bush offered a gentle perspective on the nature of presidential regrets. "When you sit behind that desk, every choice you make has consequences, and not all of them are good," the elder statesman remarked. "You make the best decisions you can with the information you have, but you carry the outcomes with you forever."

Clinton nodded in agreement, adding a final piece of advice for future occupant of the White House: "The hardest part of the job isn't making decisions when the choices are clear. It's living with the consequences when every available option is bad."

**WASHINGTON** — In a rare and candid moment of political reflection, America’s fraternity of living presidents is opening up about the missteps of their respective tenures, offering a sobering playbook of lessons to President-elect Barack Obama as he prepares to assume office amidst historic economic and foreign policy challenges.

The public reflections and private briefings mark a traditional, yet unusually urgent, passing of the torch. With the nation fighting two wars and grappling with the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, the "Presidents' Club"—a group defined by its hyper-exclusive membership and shared scars—is emphasizing humility, adaptability, and the dangers of presidential isolation.

### Lessons in Humility and Rhetoric

As outgoing President George W. Bush prepares to leave office, his recent exit interviews have carried a reflective tone rarely seen during his eight years in the White House. Bush has openly acknowledged misjudgments, specifically pointing to divisive rhetoric and operational failures during his administration.

"I regret the rhetoric," Bush admitted in a recent interview, citing his use of phrases like "bring 'em on" during the Iraq War and the "Mission Accomplished" banner aboard the USS *Abraham Lincoln* in 2003. "It conveyed a message that I wasn't sophisticated, or that I was eager for war."

Bush also pointed to the botched federal response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005 as a lesson in the perils of slow crisis management—a warning that resonates deeply as Obama prepares to manage the sprawling federal response to the ongoing economic collapse.

Bush's advice to Obama has reportedly focused on the heavy burden of the commander-in-chief role: "You’ve got to be prepared to make decisions based on what you think is right, not what is politically popular at the moment," Bush noted following a historic gathering of all living presidents at the Oval Office earlier this month.

### The Pitfalls of Overreach and Distraction

Former President Bill Clinton, whose early administration was stymied by legislative setbacks including the collapse of his healthcare reform bill, has urged Obama to protect his political capital and maintain a clear, laser-like focus.

Speaking at a public forum recently, Clinton reflected on his own early mistakes, admitting that trying to do too much too fast alienated potential allies in Congress. 

"The temptation when you come in with a big mandate is to try to push every door open at once," Clinton said. "My advice to the incoming president is to pick your top priorities—in his case, the economy—and align all your political capital behind them. Don't let the noise of Washington pull you off course."

Clinton also warned against the subtle danger of presidential exhaustion, noting that decision-making suffers when a leader is fatigued. "The White House is a pressure cooker. You have to force yourself to step back and listen to dissenting voices outside your inner circle."

### Unpredictability and the Limits of Power

For former President George H.W. Bush, the primary lesson offered to the incoming administration is the reality that events, rather than agendas, often define a presidency. Despite overseeing the fall of the Berlin Wall and a decisive victory in the Gulf War, the elder Bush’s presidency was ultimately derailed by a domestic recession—a fate he cautions Obama to remain vigilant against.

"You can have the best-laid plans, but the world gets a vote," the elder Bush remarked during a recent panel on the presidency. "What matters most is how you react to the crisis you *didn't* see coming."

Meanwhile, former President Jimmy Carter emphasized the moral weight of the office and the danger of groupthink. Reflecting on the Iranian hostage crisis that defined the end of his term, Carter stressed the importance of questioning intelligence and remaining open to diplomatic alternatives.

"The hardest thing in the world is to resist the pressure to act precipitously when the public is demanding immediate action," Carter said.

### A Receptive Audience

For his part, Obama has actively sought out the counsel of his predecessors, breaking bread with former rival John McCain, consulting frequently with Clinton, and praising George W. Bush for facilitating a smooth transition.

"Every one of these men understands a level of pressure that nobody else in the world can truly comprehend," Obama told reporters following his meeting with the former presidents. "To hear their perspectives—not just on what went right, but on what they wish they had done differently—is invaluable."

As Obama prepares to take the oath of office, the collective message from those who came before him is clear: the theory of the presidency vanishes the moment the door closes on the Oval Office. Success, they suggest, depends not on avoiding mistakes entirely, but on learning from them quickly enough to endure the next crisis.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed article based on this event: Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush appear together at the National Automobile Dealers Association forum to talk about their presidency regrets, specifically regarding Desert Storm, Middle East peace, and health care.
counterfactuals.output:
**SAN FRANCISCO** — Decades after competing in one of the most consequential presidential elections in modern American history, former adversaries Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush shared a stage before thousands of car executives and franchise owners at the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA) annual convention. 

What was billed as a marquee keynote address quickly transformed into an unusually candid, reflective masterclass in presidential history. Seated side-by-side in overstuffed armchairs, the 41st and 42nd Presidents of the United States bypassed routine political talking points to offer a rare, vulnerable look into the burdens of the Oval Office. 

Moderated before an audience accustomed to discussions on profit margins and inventory, the two elder statesmen engaged in a wide-ranging dialogue dominated by a shared motif: the heavy weight of presidential regret. Specifically, Bush and Clinton opened up about three of the defining issues of their respective terms—Operation Desert Storm, the missteps of healthcare reform, and the heartbreaking, elusive quest for peace in the Middle East.

---

### **George H.W. Bush: The Shadow of Desert Storm**

For George H.W. Bush, the 1991 Gulf War remains a high-water mark of international diplomacy and military precision. Yet, standing before the NADA crowd, the 41st President reflected on the lingering pain and geopolitical fallout of Operation Desert Storm.

Bush defended his decision not to send American troops into Baghdad to overthrow Saddam Hussein, noting that exceeding the United Nations mandate would have fractured the fragile international coalition he had meticulously assembled. However, he expressed deep, enduring regret over the immediate aftermath of the ceasefire.

"The hardest part," Bush admitted, his voice softening, "was watching what happened right after we stopped."

Following the coalition’s victory, Bush had publicly encouraged Iraqis to rise up against the regime. When Shiite insurgents in the south and Kurdish rebels in the north answered the call, Hussein’s forces responded with brutal, unchecked violence, using helicopter gunships to massacre thousands. Bush reflected on the agony of watching the human cost unfold while bound by international agreements and the fear of dragging the U.S. into an open-ended urban quagmire.

While history often credits Bush with strategic restraint, the former president acknowledged the moral toll of leaving the Iraqi dictator in power—a decision that would cast a long shadow over American foreign policy for the next decade and ultimately lead to the 2003 invasion ordered by his son, President George W. Bush.

---

### **Bill Clinton: The Missteps of Healthcare Reform**

When the conversation turned to home soil, Bill Clinton was equally candid about the greatest domestic failure of his early presidency: the collapse of his 1993 healthcare reform initiative.

Taking full ownership of the defeat, Clinton reflected on the tactical and political errors that derailed the effort. "We got arrogant," Clinton conceded. "We tried to do too much, too fast, and we did it behind closed doors."

Clinton acknowledged that appointing a massive task force—headed by First Lady Hillary Clinton—and attempting to deliver a complex, 1,000-page bill without securing broad, bipartisan support from the outset alienated both moderate Republicans and members of his own party. The resulting political backlash contributed significantly to the "Republican Revolution" of 1994, in which Democrats lost control of the House and Senate for the first time in 40 years.

Clinton told the audience that the experience taught him his most valuable lesson in governance: the necessity of incremental progress and coalition-building. "I wanted to fix the whole system in one swing," Clinton said. "I learned the hard way that in American politics, half a loaf is better than no bread at all, especially when people's lives are on the line."

---

### **A Shared Heartbreak: The Elusive Middle East Peace**

If there was a moment in the forum where the shared burden of the presidency was most palpable, it was during the discussion of Middle East peace. Both men had invested immense personal capital and diplomatic energy into bringing Israelis and Palestinians to the negotiating table—Bush through the historic 1991 Madrid Conference, and Clinton through the Oslo Accords and the 2000 Camp David Summit.

Clinton offered a raw, vivid account of the final months of his presidency, when he pushed Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to accept a historic two-state solution. Barak had agreed to unprecedented concessions, including a Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip with its capital in East Jerusalem. Arafat, however, walked away.

"I tried every single day until the last minute of my presidency," Clinton recalled, visibly still stung by the memory. "Arafat called me right before I left office and told me I was a great man. I told him, 'I am not a great man. I am a failure, and you made me one.'"

Bush echoed Clinton’s frustration, lamenting how close the region had come to a breakthrough, only to devolve back into a cycle of violence and the Second Intifada. Both former commanders-in-chief agreed that the failure to secure a lasting peace in the Holy Land remained perhaps their most tragic, unfulfilled ambition.

---

### **The Legacy of an Unlikely Friendship**

Beyond the historical revelations, what struck the NADA audience most was the deep, genuine affection between the two men. The fierce rivals of the 1992 election—a campaign defined by sharp personal attacks—had transformed into close friends, spurred by their joint efforts leading humanitarian relief for the 2004 Asian tsunami and Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

Throughout the panel, the two traded gentle barbs and fond memories, providing a stark contrast to the increasingly polarized political landscape of the modern era.

As the forum drew to a close, the applause from the audience was not merely for the history lesson, but for the rare display of presidential humility. By sharing their greatest regrets, George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton reminded those in attendance that leadership is defined not just by victories, but by the courage to look back at one’s failures—and the grace to learn from them together.

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton share the stage for a candid forum on presidential missteps.
* Bush 41 reflects on communication failures and the political fallout of his famous tax pledge.
* Clinton cites foreign policy inaction, calling the 1994 Rwandan genocide his "greatest regret."
* The former political rivals emphasize that bipartisanship and humility are essential for effective leadership.

***

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** In a rare and candid display of post-presidential camaraderie, former rivals George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton took the stage together to reflect on the heaviest burden of the Oval Office: making mistakes on the global stage.

The joint forum, which brought together the 41st and 42nd commanders-in-chief, offered an unprecedented look at how two men who once fought bitterly for the presidency now view their time in power through the lens of hindsight. 

Despite their fiercely competitive 1992 election battle, the duo demonstrated a warm rapport, using their shared platform to deliver a message on humility, public service, and the weight of executive decision-making.

### Bush on Economic Miscalculations and Broken Promises

Opening the discussion on domestic policy, George H.W. Bush reflected on what many historians consider the turning point of his presidency—his 1988 campaign pledge, "Read my lips: no new taxes," which he ultimately broke in a 1990 budget deal with a Democratic-led Congress.

"You make decisions based on what you believe is right for the country at that exact moment, even when you know the political cost will be devastating," Bush said. "Looking back, my biggest mistake wasn't doing the budget deal—it was the way I communicated it. I let the politics get ahead of the policy, and I paid the price for it at the ballot box."

Bush also acknowledged struggling to connect emotionally with the American public during the economic downturn of the early 1990s. 

"I was never much for the 'vision thing,' as people called it," Bush admitted with a self-deprecating smile. "I believed the work spoke for itself. But in the presidency, if you don't tell your story, your opponents will tell it for you."

### Clinton’s 'Greatest Regret': Inaction in Rwanda

When the conversation turned to foreign policy, Bill Clinton did not hesitate to point to the 1994 Rwandan genocide as the most painful failure of his administration. 

"If I could go back and change one thing, it would be our speed and resolve during the crisis in Rwanda," Clinton said, his voice dropping. "We were so focused on the fallout from Somalia that we failed to see the catastrophe unfolding right in front of us. Hundreds of thousands of lives were lost because we didn't act fast enough. That inaction remains the greatest regret of my presidency."

Clinton also addressed his administration's early domestic stumbles, specifically the failed 1993 health care reform effort led by then-First Lady Hillary Clinton. 

"We overreached," Clinton conceded. "We tried to do too much, too fast, without building the necessary bipartisan bridge first. I misread the mandate. You can't lead the American people down a path if you haven't brought them along in the conversation."

### A Model for Modern Politics

While the forum focused heavily on policy missteps, the overarching theme of the event was the deep, unlikely friendship that developed between the two men years after leaving office—a bond forged during their joint humanitarian work following the 2004 Asian tsunami and Hurricane Katrina.

Clinton praised his predecessor for his grace during the 1992 transition, noting that Bush had left him a warm, encouraging note in the Oval Office despite the bitter campaign. 

"George set the standard for how a former president should behave," Clinton remarked. "He showed me that at the end of the day, we are all on Team America. Our political differences are real, but our shared love for this country has to be bigger."

Bush echoed the sentiment, offering a final piece of advice for future occupant of the White House. 

"You’re going to make mistakes. Every president does," Bush said. "The test isn't whether you make them; it’s whether you have the humility to admit them, learn from them, and keep moving the country forward."

***

*CNN’s Political Unit contributed to this report.*
